sources.excerpt: When evaluating different settings (“hyperparameters”) for estimators, such as the C setting that must be manually set for an SVM, there is still a risk of overfitting on the test set because the parameters can be tweaked until the estimator performs optimally. This way, knowledge about the test set can “leak” into the model and evaluation metrics no longer report on generalization performance. To solve this problem, yet another part of the dataset can be held out as a so-called “validation set”: training proceeds on the training set, after which evaluation is done on the validation set, and when the experiment seems to be successful, final evaluation can be done on the test set.

sources.excerpt: Well calibrated classifiers are probabilistic classifiers for which the output of the predict_proba method can be directly interpreted as a confidence level. For instance, a well calibrated (binary) classifier should classify the samples such that among the samples to which it gave a predict_proba value close to, say, 0.8, approximately 80% actually belong to the positive class.
sources.inspection_note: Read original official HTML fetched for this audit. Calibration is tied to a stated positive class/event; Choice confidence cannot establish a different solver-success event. Calibration data should be disjoint from classifier fitting data.

sources.excerpt: The binomial distribution is used when there are exactly two mutually exclusive outcomes of a trial. These outcomes are appropriately labeled "success" and "failure". The binomial distribution is used to obtain the probability of observing x successes in N trials, with the probability of success on a single trial denoted by p . The binomial distribution assumes that p is fixed for all trials.  Parameter Estimation The maximum likelihood estimator of p (for fixed n ) is \( \tilde{p} = \frac{x} {n} \)
